An ecommerce merchant might sell the exact product a generative AI shopper wants and still not appear in the platform’s recommendations.
The disconnect starts with how consumers use AI chat and shopping.
For example, a shopper could specify in a single prompt the price range, size, material, compatibility, intended use, delivery date, and more.
The merchant’s job is to make those specs easy to find and verify. The task is traditional search optimization, but elevated. More than ever, today’s product data must answer questions that shoppers once had to uncover themselves.
Here are five tests to see whether AI-driven shoppers can find your product.
Identify
Can an AI shopping agent or chat understand the item?
A product listing should include the item’s name, brand, category, SKU, and, when applicable, a GTIN, UPC, EAN, or manufacturer part number. Variants identify size, color, model, or configuration.
This is basic product-data hygiene, but it’s essential for shopping agents or chats to identify matches.
In other words, establish what the product is before asking an AI system to recommend it.
Prove
Does the available product data satisfy all of a shopper’s requirements?
Imagine someone asks AI to “find waterproof hiking boots under $180 for wide feet, suitable for rocky trails, that weigh less than three pounds.”
The request contains at least five constraints:
- waterproof,
- price,
- width,
- terrain,
- weight.
A retailer might sell the perfect boot, but an AI system may not match it if the product page or catalog omits weight or width.
AI platforms both understand the complexity of this problem and see it as a way to attract shoppers. OpenAI touted its shopping system’s ability to discern complex queries in its initial shopping announcement.
Google Merchant Center specifies an attribute called [product_highlight] for important characteristics and common consumer questions. The attribute helps “customers discover information about your products across AI-driven surfaces, like AI Mode in Google Search,” according to Google’s documentation.
A useful exercise for exposing attributes and optimizing product detail pages is to list shoppers’ likely questions and then answer them in the items’ descriptions.
Verify
Can an AI agent or chat verify what the shopper will purchase and receive? A good product match is not enough if the offer itself is wrong.
Ensure that the product page, feed, cart, and checkout agree on price, availability, shipping cost, delivery timing, promotions, and purchase terms.
Google, for example, requires products in Merchant Center to match the landing page and checkout. It also recommends structured data for important offer information.
This matters when shoppers add constraints such as “under $180,” “in stock,” or “arrive by Friday.”
Supply Evidence
Can an AI shopping agent or chat find enough evidence to support a recommendation?
A product detail page should do more than assert benefits. It should give an AI shopping bot facts that explain why a product fits a shopper’s needs.
Salomon’s X Ultra 5 Mid Gore-Tex detail page is a good example. The page identifies the waterproof membrane, outsole, cushioning, fit, weight, construction, and intended terrain. It also includes multiple product images and customer reviews.
That is much more useful than a broad claim such as “built for rough weather.”
OpenAI stated that its Shopping Research feature gathers information from reviews, specifications, images, price, availability, and more, then uses those details to compare products and explain differences and tradeoffs.
The test, then, is whether the product page gives an AI shopping system enough factual support to explain the recommendation rather than repeat the retailer’s pitches.
Shop
What happens when an AI shopper describes a product that you sell?
To test, select a handful of your products and create realistic prompts based on consumer needs, not brand or product names.

Retail media may provide ecommerce retailers with high-margin revenue from an audience they have paid to attract.
Merchandise sales from online and even brick-and-mortar retailers often produce gross margins near 50%, contribution margins of 25%, and net profit approaching 12%.
Retail media margins can look much higher because merchants have incurred much of the cost of attracting shoppers. Plus, the ad buyers are often a store’s suppliers.
Products vs. Ads
Here is a comparison.
Selling a $100 product might leave $25 after cost of goods sold, fulfillment, payment processing, shipping, and other variable costs — a 25% contribution margin.
A $1,000 newsletter sponsorship has no comparable cost or return risk. Ancillary expenses such as sales commissions, creative, and technology may total $250, leaving $750 before general overhead — a 75% contribution margin.
Large retail media networks have reported similarly attractive economics. In 2022 both McKinsey & Company and Boston Consulting Group estimated operating margins from those networks at 70% and more.
Recommended
Retail Media’s Performance Dilemma
June 22, 2025
Existing Audience
Conceptually, retail media resembles advertising in the publishing industry.
A publisher attracts readers with articles, newsletters, videos, or other content and then sells advertisers access to that audience.
An ecommerce merchant attracts shoppers with products and services. Retail media monetizes the audience a retailer already has.
Consider a specialty retailer that sends four monthly newsletters to 40,000 subscribers.
A supplier agrees to pay $1,500 per month for a recurring sponsorship, hoping to drive 400 additional product sales. Selling and producing the sponsorship costs $300 per month. Thus the placement contributes about $1,200 before general overhead, or an 80% contribution margin.
The merchant emails its existing audience of subscribers.
The same logic applies to search results pages, category pages, buying guides, and other sections.
Purchase Intent
A retailer’s audience can be more valuable to advertisers than a mainstream publisher’s because shoppers are closer to a purchase.
A publisher might know that a visitor reads hiking articles. An outdoor retailer, by contrast, knows that same person searched for waterproof hiking boots, viewed several pairs, and purchased hiking socks six months ago.
That difference matters to advertisers, who are buying access to shoppers with commercial intent.
Supplier, Buyers
Supplier-funded advertising is not new to retail. Co-operative programs from suppliers have long subsidized ads that promote their products.
Retail media extends that relationship. Instead of sharing the cost of external ads, suppliers can pay the retailer directly for access to its audience.
For ecommerce merchants, it’s potentially a new revenue source from companies they know and work with.
A 2025 TransUnion study reported that 70% of retail media spending was incremental to suppliers’ broader trade budgets, meaning retail media generates new money rather than moving from one bucket to another.
Double-Dip
One final point. When the retail media buyer is a supplier, the ecommerce shop earns twice: once from ad revenue and again from higher merchandise sales.
The setup echoes co-op campaigns. The supplier wants to sell in the retail channel and doesn’t mind investing in advertising, even when the retailer gets to double-dip, profit-wise.

On July 22, 2026, France became the latest major search market to get AI Overviews.
Which means that, for once, we got to watch the before and after without having to guess. In most markets, AI Overviews crept in alongside algorithm updates and seasonal swings, and we all spent the following year arguing about how much they had really cost us. France had a launch date, and we were already tracking: 963 domains in Google Search Console, over the 28 days before the launch and the 9 days after it.
Xibeijia Guan, our data scientist, pulled and analysed the data for French sites (we explain how in the methodology at the end of this study). Less than a month after launch, Google's AI Overviews are already eating into click-through rates in France.
The domains most exposed to AI Overviews lost more than a fifth of their click-through rate in nine days. The ones barely exposed hardly moved at all.
So this isn't an algorithm update. It's AI Overviews.
Find where an AI Overview shows up in your SERPs
Use the SERP features filter to see exactly which of your rankings trigger an AI Overview. Head to the Organic keywords report in Site Explorer, then select AI Overview in the SERP features filter.
Across the domains we studied, click-through rate fell 3.4% in nine days.
For the domains most exposed to AI Overviews, it fell 23.1%. Six times as much.
And this isn't a handful of unlucky sites dragging the average down: 82.2% of highly exposed domains lost CTR. At that level of exposure, getting away with it has become the exception.
In between those two extremes, the relationship holds pretty steady. If you compare the change in CTR against each domain's AI Overview rate across all 963 domains, you get a slope of −0.9.
In other words: every extra point of AI Overview exposure costs you roughly one point of click-through rate.
If 15% of your queries trigger an AI Overview, expect to lose somewhere around 15% of your CTR. It's crude, but it's actionable: pull your exposure rate from Site Explorer and you have your order of magnitude.
Sidenote
A slope is not a prediction. Some heavily exposed sites are doing fine, and some barely exposed ones are falling apart for reasons that have nothing to do with AI. Your AI Overview rate is a risk factor, not a verdict. We'll check back in a few months to see how these sites actually fared.
Barely anyone lost rankings in late July. Pages still show up, just as often as before, sometimes more.
They just get clicked less.
It's the same pattern we found in the global study we ran in late 2025, and the same shape as the great decoupling: an AI Overview doesn't remove you from the SERP, it makes you redundant inside it. The most extreme case in our French panel had +183% impressions for −1.9% clicks, which divides its CTR by more than three.
One caveat: that −23.1% describes a minority of sites. Across the full panel, the median is −5.7% CTR and −8.8% clicks.
But that reassuring median hides a brutal distribution.
Almost one site in two lost more than 10% of its daily clicks. One in twenty lost half. In nine days.
And exposure will almost certainly keep climbing. Today the median AI Overview rate among the domains we studied is 5.4%, and 29% of them are already above 10%. Those numbers have only gone one way in every market since 2024.
The .fr domains in our panel lost 12.3% of clicks at the median, against 8.8% for the panel as a whole. French sites are more exposed than the international players competing in the same market.
One sector stands clearly apart. Health has an AI Overview rate of 22.2%, the highest in the study, and its click-through rate fell 20.4%.
Health queries are informational, they have short answers, and there's no transaction waiting at the end. That's exactly what an AI Overview absorbs best: the answer fits inside the box, and the user leaves with what they came for.
This matches our previous research into what triggers AI Overviews, where we found that 44.1% of medical queries triggered an AI Overview.
What decides your fate isn't your vertical, it's the intent behind your queries. A query that a single paragraph can answer is a query you're going to lose. A query that needs a tool, an account, a price, a purchase or a human opinion holds up far better.
Look at your keywords through that lens before you look at your industry.
That −23.1% is probably not the worst of it.
Our global research tracked the same effect over two years: the impact of AI Overviews on position 1 click-through rate went from −34.5% in spring 2025 to −58% by the end of 2025. It doesn't fade with time, it gets worse, as AI Overviews trigger on more queries and users get used to not clicking.
Nothing suggests France escapes that trajectory. We'll re-run this analysis over a longer window to see how far it goes.
The −23.1% median CTR figure is the raw observed change for the highly exposed group, with no control adjustment. Over the same period, the control group's CTR rose 2.3%. So highly exposed sites didn't just fall 23%: they also missed the small lift everyone else enjoyed. Once you account for that, the real effect of AI Overviews is −24.8%.
Two weeks after AI Overviews arrived in France, the most exposed sites had lost a fifth of their click-through rate. The least exposed felt nothing at all. In between, the relationship is linear: roughly one point of CTR per point of exposure.
Three things to take away.
One. Your risk is measurable, and it's measurable before the damage is done. The SERP features filter in Site Explorer gives you your share of queries with an AI Overview.
Two. Stop steering by impressions. They didn't drop. Click-through rate is what took the hit.
Three. These orders of magnitude line up with what others have measured: Seer Interactive reports organic CTR declines of 49.4% to 65.2%, Kevin Indig more than 50%, Authoritas 47.5%. Nobody is measuring the opposite.
Search is going zero-click, and France has just joined the movement.

I run content for ecommerce brands. Thanks to cheap, infinite copy from generative AI, the question I’m paid to answer has changed. It used to be “Can we publish this?” Now it is “Will anyone see it?”
So my favorite content marketing tools don’t write a word. They tell me whether my writing was seen and where.
2 Systems
Search and discovery traffic now comes from Google and generative AI platforms. Ranking in one system doesn’t mean showing up in the other. An August 2025 Ahrefs analysis found that only about 12% of the links cited by ChatGPT, Perplexity, and other genAI platforms also ranked in Google’s top 10 for that search (prompt) term.
AI referrals account for only a small share of web traffic, but some benchmarks suggest they convert at a higher rate than organic search.
The way I measure content performance has shifted, too. I still watch engagement signals such as time on page and returning readers. But I also look at what happens next: product-page visits, email signups, assisted conversions, and revenue from organic or AI-referred sessions.
Increasingly, I track whether a page gets cited.
My Stack
My tools split into two layers: gathering the data, then making sense of it.
Layer one: data gathering
Google Search Console shows the queries that surface my content, providing a first-party view that paid tools can’t replicate.
Google Analytics covers behavior and traffic sources, and a simple referral filter there catches clicks from genAI platforms. Ahrefs gives me keyword, backlink, and competitor depth, plus AI-citation tracking through BrandRadar.
Otterly is my dedicated AI-visibility tracker. For about $29 a month, it answers the question I now pose weekly. “Is ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and AI Overviews citing my content?”
Screaming Frog’s SEO Spider catches potential blocks to Google and genAI crawlers before it costs me visibility.
Layer two: what it means
Claude stitches the tools together: instead of exporting five spreadsheets, I connect Ahrefs and Otterly and query Claude about the data, such as which pages Google ranks but genAI ignores.
NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook) turns data from my own exports and reports into a queryable analysis.
Notice what’s missing. None of these tools generates content.
Performance
Start with Search Console and Google Analytics. Add an optimization platform such as Ahrefs for traditional keyword, backlink, and competitor data.
Switch on Ahrefs’ AI-visibility tracking. Read the numbers as trends across repeated checks rather than a single day’s result, since the answers vary from prompt to prompt. And bring in ChatGPT, Claude, or similar to analyze the data, not to write copy.
I’ve always measured content performance, but the process now goes beyond traditional organic search rankings and conversions. I need to know whether a page is cited in AI answers, where the citations appear, and what those visitors do once they reach the site.

The retail media market is substantial and growing.
A 2025 Journal of Retailing paper estimated 2024 global retail media spending at more than $140 billion, including $54 billion in the United States. More recently, eMarketer forecasts U.S. retail media ad spend at $69.33 billion in 2026, a 17.9% increase from 2025.
Using Retail Media
Ecommerce companies can participate on either side of the retail media market.
A merchant selling through Amazon, Walmart, or other marketplaces can buy ads to convert more shoppers.
The same merchant can also sell and publish ads on its own site and email list.
For the advertiser, retail media can be useful because the message appears close to the purchase decision. A shopper searching for “waterproof hiking boots” shows a strong purchase intent.
Value Creation
Imagine a brand that spends $1,000 on retail media and generates $5,000 in sales it would not otherwise have received. If those sales produce $1,500 in contribution margin before advertising, the campaign generated $500 in net benefit.
That is value creation.
The economics look different when the sale would have happened anyway.
Imagine a marketplace where a seller historically ranked well organically. The marketplace adds more sponsored placements, competitors bid for them, and the seller must spend $5 on advertising to maintain a $50 sale it used to get without that expense.
- The marketplace earns $5 more.
- The seller earns $5 less.
- The shopper still purchases the same product.
Retail media has generated revenue for the marketplace, but not for the advertiser.
This possibility is more than theoretical. The Journal of Retailing report noted concerns that retail media can erode advertisers’ margins when the attributed sales are not incremental or new.
Lowers Profit
Moreover, retail media can erode the margins of merchants publishing the ads
Consider a retailer with a category page generating $100,000 in monthly merchandise sales and $30,000 in gross profit.
A supplier agrees to pay $3,000 per month for a prominent advertising placement, seemingly elevating margins to $33,000.
But suppose the sponsored placement displaces the merchant’s own conversions. Gross profit falls from $30,000 to $28,000.
The retailer-publisher collected $3,000 in media revenue but gained only $1,000 overall.
Even worse, if gross profit from product sales falls to $26,000, the $3,000 from retail media lowered overall margin by $1,000.
Advertising revenue increased. Business performance declined.
That risk extends beyond a single product. Too many sponsored products or irrelevant recommendations could make a store harder to shop, weaken customer trust, or reduce conversions over time.
For marketplace advertisers, return on ad spend cannot alone justify the investment. An advertiser generating $8 in sales for every $1 ad may have received those conversions anyway.
The more useful measure is whether the advertising changed the outcome.
To estimate the effect, large advertisers use randomized experiments, marketing mix models, geo-testing, and similar methods. Smaller companies can assess new-customer sales, organic performance, and periods with and without campaigns.
Incremental Value
Thus retail media is not inherently a win or loss.
If it creates profitable new demand for advertisers, it’s a win. If it adds cost to conversions advertisers would have received anyway, it’s a loss.
For retailer-publishers, it adds value only if it produces a higher net margin.
That distinction matters for both sides of retail media.

Ecommerce companies may soon compete not only for shoppers, but also to “own” the AI through which those shoppers buy.
Conceptually, the idea is not new. Competing for customers has long included competing for attention and proxies. Take search engine optimization. Ecommerce marketers work hard to rank in search engine result pages to win a shopper. The search engine is a proxy.
Generative engine optimization seeks similar visibility, but another layer of AI shopping is emerging.
Commerce Agents
On September 2, Anthropic released “Building Commerce Agents with Claude,” a collection of software patterns, “guardrails,” and implementations to help companies build AI agents for retail and other commerce applications.
The blueprint includes two examples.
Shopping agent
First, there is a consumer-facing shopping agent. This agent resides on a store’s website or app and connects to the product data, checkout software, and other services.
Claude poses an example. A shopper could tell the agent she needs a tent, sleeping bag, and stove for a weekend trip with two children. The agent would search the store’s product catalog, select compatible items, compare those products, and add them to the shopping cart, all while considering the customer’s preferences and previous orders.
After the sale, the same shopping agent could answer questions about delivery, returns, exchanges, and refunds.
Claude claims retailers (unnamed) running its shopping agents have experienced a 35% increase in order value and a 60% improvement in conversion rate.
The claim is interesting given that many enterprise retailers have deployed similar agents.
Merchant agent
Anthropic’s second example agent works behind the scenes with a store’s internal systems.
An ecommerce manager could ask the agent which products to discount to clear old inventory and free up cash. The merchant agent might analyze inventory levels, track sales velocity, recommend price changes, and even draft marketing campaigns in response.
The blueprint’s guardrails would require human approval before the merchant agent could implement significant changes.
Similar merchant agents already exist in some ecommerce platforms, but the Anthropic blueprint should make it relatively easier to build custom implementations.
Shoppers Want AI
Anthropic’s announcement comes as more consumers appear willing to involve AI in shopping during the 2026 Christmas season.
Bain & Company, an Anthropic partner, commissioned an August survey of 1,105 U.S. shoppers for its holiday 2026 forecast. Twenty-four percent of online buyers plan to start their holiday shopping on AI platforms such as Claude, Google Gemini, and ChatGPT, up from 17% in 2025.
Roughly 60% of respondents plan to start on retail or brand websites, up from 51% last year.
The two findings are not necessarily contradictory.
Some shoppers may ask ChatGPT or Gemini what to buy before visiting a store. Others may go directly to a merchant’s site and use its AI agent instead of search or navigation menus.
Still others might use both an external and on-site agent during the same purchase.
2 Models
Bain’s survey describes two emerging models for AI commerce.
In the first, an external platform owns the AI relationship or at least the shopping interface. ChatGPT, Perplexity, or another assistant finds products from multiple sellers and helps complete the transaction.
Shopper → AI platform → Merchant
OpenAI, for example, introduced Instant Checkout with Stripe and the Agentic Commerce Protocol in 2025, allowing supported purchases without leaving ChatGPT.
Google has taken a similar approach with its Universal Commerce Protocol, developed with Shopify, Etsy, Wayfair, Target, Walmart, and others. The protocol connects AI experiences with existing merchant and payment infrastructure.
The second agentic shopping model puts the merchant closer to the center.
Shopper → Merchant’s AI → Merchant
Anthropic’s blueprint helps make this approach practical. A retailer can offer conversational product discovery while retaining its own catalog, checkout, customer relationship, and brand experience.
Ecommerce may be entering a race to own the AI through which customers shop.
Customer Relationships
Piece by piece and innovation by innovation, the industry is assembling an agentic AI commerce stack. As these two AI shopping models emerge, direct customer relationships will likely become increasingly important.
Merchants that know their customers, retain first-party data, and maintain direct channels such as email, loyalty programs, and on-site experiences should be better positioned — whether shoppers arrive through an outside AI platform or use the merchant’s own agent.
